properties.name: Trajan
properties.one_line: The 63-year-old emperor died here around 8-9 August, worn out and dropsical after abandoning the failed siege of Hatra; the news broke at Antioch on 11 August, the day this map is set.

properties.name: Hadrian
properties.one_line: The 41-year-old legate of Syria was acclaimed emperor by the legions at Antioch on 11 August, the exact day this map is frozen on.

properties.name: Plotina
properties.one_line: Trajan's widow stood at his deathbed at Selinus and, according to hostile later gossip, helped secure Hadrian's succession in the confused hours afterward.

properties.name: Matidia
properties.one_line: Trajan's niece traveled with the imperial party and was present when he died at Selinus, then accompanied his ashes back toward Rome.

properties.name: Vibia Sabina
properties.location_117: Antioch, Syria (probable location, traveling with Hadrian's household)
properties.one_line: Hadrian's wife, married to him since 100, became empress this year as part of a household that had been based with him in the eastern provinces.

properties.name: Publius Acilius Attianus
properties.one_line: Hadrian's former guardian and joint praetorian prefect stood at Trajan's deathbed and announced Hadrian's adoption and succession on 9 August.

properties.name: Pliny the Younger
properties.location_117: Laurentine villa, near Ostia (probable site near modern Castel Fusano)
properties.one_line: Pliny was already dead by this year, his last securely dated letters written from Bithynia-Pontus around 113; his seaside villa near Ostia stood empty of him in 117.

properties.name: Pliny the Younger
properties.location_117: Tuscan villa near Tifernum Tiberinum (modern Città di Castello)
properties.one_line: Pliny's inland estate above the Tiber, described lovingly in his letters, sat unattended in 117, its owner already several years dead.

properties.name: Tacitus
properties.one_line: The 61-year-old former consul and proconsul of Asia was in Rome working on the Annals, having recently finished circulating the Histories.

properties.name: Suetonius
properties.one_line: Suetonius held the posts of director of the imperial libraries and keeper of the archives under Trajan and continued in the post as Hadrian's reign opened, based in Rome rather than at the front.

properties.name: Plutarch
properties.location_117: Chaeronea, Boeotia (holding a lifelong priesthood at nearby Delphi since c. 95)
properties.one_line: The 71-year-old author of the Parallel Lives lived out his final years in his native Chaeronea while still holding his Delphic priesthood.

properties.name: Epictetus
properties.one_line: The formerly enslaved Stoic, about 62 this year, ran his well-known philosophical school at Nicopolis, drawing students from across the Greek and Roman elite.

properties.name: Juvenal
properties.one_line: Juvenal was in Rome finishing Book Two of his Satires, including Satire 6, published around this year.

properties.name: Rufus of Ephesus
properties.one_line: Rufus practiced and wrote medical treatises at Ephesus; ancient sources place his active years under Trajan, though his exact dates remain debated among historians of medicine.

properties.name: Soranus of Ephesus
properties.one_line: The Ephesus-born physician practiced medicine in Rome across the reigns of Trajan and Hadrian, later writing the influential Gynaecology.

properties.name: Arrian
properties.one_line: The roughly 31-year-old Bithynian was studying under Epictetus at Nicopolis around this time, taking the notes that would become the Discourses, decades before his own career as historian and general.

properties.name: Favorinus of Arles
properties.one_line: The Gaulish-born sophist had already built a reputation in Rome and Athens by this year and was moving in the circle that would soon include the new emperor Hadrian.

properties.name: Titus Statilius Crito
properties.location_117: Selinus, Cilicia (probable, attending the dying emperor)
properties.one_line: Trajan's own physician since the Dacian campaigns, known to the Suda as Criton of Heraclea and author of a lost history of those wars called the Getica, was probably still attending the emperor when he died at Selinus.

properties.name: Rabbi Akiva
properties.one_line: In his sixties, Akiva ran his academy at Bnei Brak while the Kitos War burned through nearby Lydda and the wider Jewish diaspora.

properties.name: Rabban Gamaliel II
properties.one_line: The patriarch of the Sanhedrin was caught up in the distress at Lydda during Lusius Quietus's siege of the town, and would die within the year.

properties.name: Ignatius of Antioch
properties.location_117: Rome (site of martyrdom; died c. 108, roughly a decade before this snapshot)
properties.one_line: Ignatius was already dead by this year, condemned to the beasts in Rome's arena around 108 after writing his seven letters on the journey from Antioch.

properties.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
properties.one_line: About 48 years old, Polycarp was already established as bishop of Smyrna, a position he is attested to have held by this year at the latest.

properties.name: Lusius Quietus
properties.one_line: Trajan's Berber cavalry commander, fresh off crushing the Jewish revolt in Mesopotamia, was appointed governor of Judaea in 117 and moved to besiege the rebels holding Lydda.

properties.name: Quintus Marcius Turbo
properties.one_line: Marcius Turbo led a combined land and naval force that crushed the Jewish revolt in Egypt and Cyrenaica through 117, driving the rebel Lukuas out of Alexandria.

properties.name: Lukuas
properties.location_117: Fleeing toward Judaea after the fall of the Cyrenaica-Egypt revolt
properties.one_line: The Jewish rebel leader Cassius Dio calls Andreas, and Eusebius calls a self-styled king, burned Alexandria before being driven out by Marcius Turbo and fleeing east toward Judaea in 117.
